blocks.text: At a routine visit at 34 weeks, the midwife measures a symphysis-fundal height of 29 cm, which is 5 cm below what the dates predict. The woman has no symptoms, but the baby may be small, may be healthy, or may be failing to thrive because of placental insufficiency. A tape measure, an ultrasound scan, a screening test and a cardiotocograph (CTG) each answer a different part of that question, and each has limits that you must understand.

blocks.markdown: Fetal assessment has three goals: confirm **growth**, detect **structural or chromosomal anomaly** and judge **wellbeing** (whether the fetus is receiving enough oxygen). Every tool can be placed on a spectrum from *screening* (identifies who is at higher risk) to *diagnostic* (gives a yes or no answer). Confusing the two is the commonest conceptual mistake in this topic.

blocks.title: Symphysis-fundal height (SFH)
blocks.text: SFH is the distance in centimetres from the upper border of the pubic symphysis to the top of the uterine fundus, measured with a non-elastic tape from 24 weeks of gestation with the measurement markings facing away from the examiner. Between about 24 and 36 weeks the SFH in cm approximates the gestation in weeks, within about 2 to 3 cm. It is plotted on a centile chart, ideally customised, at each antenatal visit.

blocks.markdown: A measurement more than 3 cm below expectation, a static or slowly rising plot, or a measurement above the 90th centile prompts a **growth ultrasound**. SFH is a screening tool with limited sensitivity: obesity, fibroids, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy and fetal lie all affect it. On ultrasound, **biometry** records the **biparietal diameter, head circumference, abdominal circumference (AC) and femur length**. These are combined (for example by the Hadlock formula) to give an **estimated fetal weight (EFW)**, which is plotted on a centile chart. Dating by crown-rump length is used between about 11+2 and 14+1 weeks, and by head circumference after that. A fetus below the 10th centile is **small for gestational age (SGA)**; one below the 3rd centile or with abnormal Doppler is at higher risk. The **abdominal circumference** is the most sensitive single measure of growth restriction because it reflects liver glycogen and fat stores. **Fetal growth restriction (FGR)** implies a failure to reach genetic growth potential, usually because of placental insufficiency, and is supported by **umbilical artery Doppler** showing raised resistance, absent or reversed end-diastolic flow.

blocks.markdown: **Principles and limits of screening.** A screening test estimates risk; it does not diagnose. It is judged by **sensitivity** (the proportion of affected pregnancies detected), the **false-positive rate** and the **positive predictive value (PPV)**, which depends strongly on how common the condition is. A woman must be able to give informed consent, understand that she may decline, and know that a higher-chance result leads to a choice between further screening, diagnostic testing or no further action. The anomaly scan cannot detect all anomalies, and a normal result does not guarantee a healthy baby. In the UK, a combined-test result with a chance of 1 in 150 or higher is classed as higher chance.

blocks.title: Positive predictive value of a screening test
blocks.prompt: A screening test for a chromosomal condition has a detection rate of 90 percent and a false-positive rate of 5 percent. The condition affects 1 in 500 pregnancies. Of 10 000 women screened, what proportion of screen-positive women truly have the condition?

steps.text: True positives: 90 percent of 20. False positives: 5 percent of the 9 980 unaffected.
Positive predictive value is true positives divided by all positives.

blocks.answer: About 3.5 percent, so most screen-positive women do not have an affected fetus, and a diagnostic test is needed.

blocks.markdown: **Cardiotocography (CTG)** records the fetal heart rate and uterine contractions simultaneously. **Indications** include high-risk pregnancy or labour (continuous monitoring), abnormal findings on intermittent auscultation, reduced fetal movements after 28 weeks (an antenatal CTG), suspected placental insufficiency and abnormal liquor volume. Interpretation follows the **DR C BRAVADO** structure: Define Risk, Contractions, Baseline rate, Variability, Accelerations, Decelerations, Overall impression. Features are classed in UK practice as normal, suspicious or pathological.

rows: Less than 5 beats per minute for 50 minutes or more is abnormal
Present, at least 15 beats per minute for 15 seconds
Absence alone is of uncertain significance
None, or early decelerations that mirror contractions
Variable, late (after the peak of the contraction) or prolonged decelerations
blocks.caption: Basic CTG features.

blocks.title: Interpreting a CTG
blocks.prompt: A woman in labour has a CTG showing a baseline of 150 beats per minute, variability of 3 beats per minute for 55 minutes and repeated late decelerations after each contraction. How should it be interpreted?

steps.text: Baseline: 150 beats per minute is within 110 to 160, so the baseline is normal.
Variability: 3 beats per minute is below 5 and has lasted more than 50 minutes, which is abnormal.
Decelerations: late decelerations begin after the peak of the contraction and are characteristic of uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia.

Overall: reduced variability together with late decelerations is pathological. Act urgently: reposition, stop oxytocin, correct hypotension, assess for a cause, consider fetal blood sampling or expedite delivery.

blocks.answer: A pathological CTG suggestive of fetal hypoxia that needs urgent action and consideration of delivery.

items: SFH screens for growth problems; biometry and Doppler confirm them.
AC is the most sensitive growth measure; reduced liquor and abnormal Doppler support placental insufficiency.
Combined and cell-free DNA tests give risk, not a diagnosis; amniocentesis and CVS give a diagnosis but carry a miscarriage risk.
CTG interpretation needs baseline, variability, accelerations and decelerations in context.

blocks.title: Risk is not diagnosis
blocks.text: A higher-chance screening result simply changes the probability. Whether to proceed to diagnostic testing is the woman's choice, informed by the PPV of the test and the small risk of the invasive procedure.

points: Symphysis-fundal height after 24 weeks approximates gestational age in weeks and prompts growth ultrasound when it deviates by more than 3 cm.

Ultrasound biometry uses head circumference, abdominal circumference and femur length; abdominal circumference is the most sensitive for growth restriction and umbilical artery Doppler assesses placental resistance.
Screening estimates risk and has false positives and false negatives; CVS and amniocentesis are diagnostic but carry a miscarriage risk.
CTG is interpreted by baseline, variability, accelerations and decelerations; late decelerations with reduced variability suggest hypoxia.

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks has a symphysis-fundal height of 26 cm that has plotted below the 10th centile on two consecutive visits. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound scan for fetal biometry and growth

questions.correctOptionText: Arrange an ultrasound scan for fetal biometry and growth

distractorRationale.a: A persistently low SFH should not be reassured away.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: SFH is a screening tool and growth ultrasound is the next test.
distractorRationale.c: Amniocentesis is for suspected chromosomal anomaly, not isolated small SFH.
distractorRationale.d: Induction is not indicated without evidence of compromise.

questions.explanation: An SFH more than 3 cm below dates or plotting below the 10th centile suggests possible growth restriction. Ultrasound biometry and Doppler then confirm whether the fetus is small and whether placental resistance is raised.

questions.stem: Which single ultrasound measurement is the most sensitive for detecting fetal growth restriction?

distractorRationale.a: The head is spared in asymmetrical growth restriction (brain sparing), so BPD changes late.
distractorRationale.b: Femur length is relatively preserved early.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: it reflects liver size and subcutaneous fat, which fall first with placental insufficiency.
distractorRationale.d: Nuchal translucency is a first-trimester screening marker for aneuploidy.

questions.explanation: In placental insufficiency the fetus redistributes blood to the brain, so abdominal organs and fat stores fall behind earlier than the head. This makes the abdominal circumference the most sensitive single biometric parameter.

questions.stem: A woman at 13 weeks has a combined test chance of trisomy 21 of 1 in 90. Which statement is the most accurate counselling?

options.text: The baby definitely has Down syndrome
This is a higher-chance result; she can choose cell-free DNA testing or a diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis), or no further testing
The test is normal because the risk is below 1 in 2

questions.correctOptionText: This is a higher-chance result; she can choose cell-free DNA testing or a diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis), or no further testing

distractorRationale.b: Correct: 1 in 90 exceeds the 1 in 150 threshold and the options include further screening, diagnosis or declining.
distractorRationale.c: Testing is voluntary and informed choice is required.
distractorRationale.d: Risk is compared with the programme threshold, not with 1 in 2.

questions.explanation: A chance of 1 in 90 is higher than 1 in 150, so she is offered further choices. Screening provides probability rather than diagnosis, and each option has its own accuracy and risk.

questions.stem: A woman receives a positive cell-free DNA result for trisomy 18. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The result is diagnostic and no further testing is required
The result is a highly accurate screening result, and diagnostic testing is offered to confirm
The result excludes all structural anomalies
The result is invalid after 20 weeks

questions.correctOptionText: The result is a highly accurate screening result, and diagnostic testing is offered to confirm

distractorRationale.a: cfDNA is from placental DNA and can be discordant, so it is not diagnostic.
distractorRationale.c: It tests only common aneuploidies, not structural anomalies.
distractorRationale.d: Cell-free DNA tests remain valid later in pregnancy.

questions.explanation: Cell-free DNA mostly derives from the placenta, so false positives from confined placental mosaicism occur. Confirmation by CVS or amniocentesis is therefore offered before irreversible decisions.

questions.stem: A CTG shows a baseline of 140 beats per minute, variability of 10 beats per minute, two accelerations in 20 minutes and no decelerations. Which description is correct?

options.text: Pathological because of the baseline rate

distractorRationale.a: Correct: baseline 110 to 160, variability 5 to 25, accelerations present and no decelerations.
distractorRationale.c: 10 beats per minute is within 5 to 25.

questions.explanation: Every feature is within normal limits: baseline 140, variability 10, accelerations present and no decelerations. This pattern indicates an intact autonomic response and oxygenated fetus.

questions.stem: True or false: A CTG with variability of 3 beats per minute lasting 60 minutes is reassuring.
questions.explanation: Reduced variability (below 5 beats per minute) lasting 50 minutes or more is abnormal because it implies impaired autonomic control, often through hypoxia or acidaemia. It requires urgent senior review, not reassurance.

questions.stem: A screening test for a condition has a detection rate of 85 percent and a false-positive rate of 2 percent. The condition affects 1 in 250 pregnancies. In 10 000 women screened, calculate the positive predictive value as a percentage (answer in percent, to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: Affected pregnancies are 10 000 divided by 250, giving 40, so true positives are 0.85 times 40, which is 34. False positives are 0.02 times 9 960, which is 199.2, so PPV is 34 divided by 233.2, or about 14.6 percent.

questions.stem: Intermittent auscultation after a contraction counts 74 fetal heart beats over 30 seconds. Calculate the fetal heart rate in beats per minute.
questions.explanation: Doubling 74 beats counted over 30 seconds gives 148 beats per minute. This is within the normal baseline range of 110 to 160 beats per minute.

questions.stem: A midwife measures the symphysis-fundal height at 30 weeks as 36 cm, well above the 90th centile. Explain how SFH is measured, what it is used for and its limitations, and how this woman should be managed.
markingGuide: Measured from the top of the pubic symphysis to the top of the fundus with a non-elastic tape, markings facing away, from 24 weeks
Approximates gestation in weeks within about 2 to 3 cm and is plotted on a centile chart
Screening tool with limited sensitivity: affected by obesity, fibroids, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy and fetal lie

A discrepancy of more than 3 cm (here 6 cm above expected) triggers an ultrasound; causes include macrosomia, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy, fibroids and wrong dates, and glucose testing for diabetes is considered
Biometry (head circumference, abdominal circumference, femur length) with estimated fetal weight
Ultrasound biometry, liquor volume and number of fetuses guide further management
questions.explanation: SFH is a simple first-line screen, so a large discrepancy leads to ultrasound confirmation rather than action on the tape alone. Biometry and liquor volume then separate a large baby from polyhydramnios or a multiple pregnancy.

questions.stem: Discuss the principles and limits of antenatal screening for chromosomal and structural anomalies, using the combined test and the anomaly scan as examples.
markingGuide: Screening estimates the chance of a condition; it does not diagnose
Combined test uses nuchal translucency, free beta-hCG, PAPP-A and maternal age at 11+2 to 14+1 weeks
Sensitivity, false-positive rate and PPV; PPV depends on prevalence so most screen-positive results are unaffected
Higher-chance result leads to further screening (cell-free DNA) or diagnostic testing (CVS, amniocentesis) with miscarriage risk about 0.5 to 1 percent
Anomaly scan at 18+0 to 20+6 weeks detects many but not all structural anomalies, and quality depends on fetal position and maternal habitus
Informed choice, consent and the right to decline; counselling before and after testing
questions.explanation: Screening reduces uncertainty without removing it, so its value lies in giving women informed options. The distinction between screening and diagnosis, and the effect of prevalence on PPV, are central to counselling.
